name: CAM

paper.title: CAM: A Constructivist View of Agentic Memory for LLM-Based Reading Comprehension

construction.unit: text chunk (256 or 512 tokens) as a graph node; LLM summary node per cluster at each higher level
construction.kept_as: raw chunks kept verbatim + LLM summaries of overlapping chunk clusters
construction.processing: link chunks by embedding similarity mixed with position; copy nodes that bridge separate neighbour groups; label propagation clusters; LLM summarises each cluster; recurse

organization.structure: multi-level graph: chunk graph at level 0, cluster-summary graphs above, a node may belong to several clusters
organization.stores: one composed graph of all levels + one embedding matrix
organization.index: dense embedding of every node at every level

management.operations: new batch: add edges for new chunks, redo replicas and labels only for affected nodes, re-summarise changed clusters, propagate upward (paper; not in released code)

retrieval.candidates: cosine top-s over all nodes of all levels (s=5 in paper, 10 in code default), then same-level neighbours and child nodes of kept nodes
retrieval.selection: LLM keeps the helpful nodes each turn; repeat until the pool stops changing or 5 turns
retrieval.budget: no cap: every node kept in any turn

use.context: all kept nodes (summaries and raw chunks, adjacent chunks joined) as numbered passages
use.reasoning: up to 5 LLM selection calls, then one answer call

classify.note: Candidates start from a dense top-s over all levels, then grow along same-level edges and down to child nodes; an LLM picks which nodes to keep at every turn.

stages.ingestion: Documents are split into chunks of 256 or 512 tokens and each chunk is embedded (text-embedding-3-small).
stages.construction: Chunks form a level-0 graph: each chunk links to at most 10 others whose score (weighted cosine similarity plus a Gaussian bonus for nearby positions) passes a threshold. Each node is copied once per connected group of its neighbours, label propagation clusters the copies, and an LLM summarises every cluster into a node of the next level.
stages.organization: Summary nodes form their own graph (linked when clusters overlap or when their members are linked) and are clustered and summarised again, giving a hierarchy where one node can feed several parents.
stages.update: For a new batch of chunks the paper only recomputes the copies and labels of affected nodes and re-summarises clusters that changed, level by level. The released code builds the whole hierarchy in one pass.
stages.retrieval: Prune-and-Grow: cosine top-s over nodes of all levels, an LLM keeps the helpful ones, their same-level neighbours and children join the pool, and the LLM picks again, until the pool stops changing or 5 turns pass.
stages.answer: The answer model reads every node kept in any turn (summaries plus raw chunks, neighbouring chunks joined) as numbered passages.

summary: Reading memory built by incremental overlapping clustering: chunks are linked by meaning and position, clustered with node copies so a chunk can feed several LLM summaries, stacked into levels, and read by an LLM that grows its selection along the graph.

headline: Memory is a stack of graphs: raw chunks at the bottom, LLM summaries of overlapping chunk clusters above; a chunk can feed several summaries.
Reading is Prune-and-Grow: an LLM keeps useful nodes from a dense top-s, the pool grows to their neighbours and children, and the LLM picks again for up to 5 turns.
The released code only builds offline, so the paper's batch-online results (Fig. 3) cannot be rerun from it.

abstract.text: CAM borrows Piaget's constructivist theory to state three properties a reading agent's memory should have: structured schemata, flexible assimilation and dynamic accommodation. It builds memory by incremental overlapping clustering: text chunks are linked by semantic similarity and position, nodes are copied so they can belong to several clusters, and each cluster is summarised by an LLM into a higher level, with new batches updating only the affected parts. At question time an LLM starts from the most similar nodes and grows its selection along the memory graph. The authors report gains over RAPTOR, GraphRAG, HippoRAG, MemTree and others on six long-text QA, summarisation and claim-verification sets, and faster batch insertion than rebuilding offline.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

write.src: paper App. E; code preprocess_chunks.py L37-L39

write.how: score every pair as α·cosine + (1−α)·exp(−(i−j)²/2σ²); each chunk links to its top-k partners with score ≥ θ
write.src: paper §4.1.1, Eq. 2, App. E; code L124-L169

write.how: for each node, take its neighbours without it; each connected group of neighbours gets its own copy of the node, and edges are rewired between copies
label propagation on the graph of copies; map copies back to nodes, so clusters overlap; clusters over the cap are cut into consecutive slices
GPT-4o-mini (temperature 0) writes a summary of each cluster's member texts; the summaries become the next level's nodes, linked by overlap or member edges
repeat split, cluster and summarise on the new level until the number of clusters no longer falls or 10 levels are reached; then merge all levels into one graph and one embedding matrix

a new batch adds edges, redoes copies only for new nodes and their neighbours, reruns label propagation from the affected copies (spreading while labels change), and re-summarises changed clusters level by level
write.note: Not in the released code, which always rebuilds from all chunks.

read.scores: embedding of every node at every level (raw chunks and summaries)
read.how: cosine similarity between the question embedding and all node embeddings; keep the top-s
GPT-4o-mini returns the list of helpful passage numbers; those nodes join the evidence
the next pool is the kept nodes plus their same-level neighbours and their children one level down
prune and grow again until the pool equals the previous one or the turn limit is hit; up to 2 retries on unparsable output
all nodes kept in any turn, sorted by id; consecutive level-0 chunks are joined into one passage; if nothing was kept, the seed nodes are used

answer_context.sees: every node the LLM kept in any turn: summaries and raw chunks
answer_context.format: "Passage i: {text}" lines under the question, in a fixed answer prompt (multiple-choice, generative, claim or summary variant)
includes: raw chunk text, consecutive chunks joined
answer_context.note: No size cap: the context grows with the number of kept nodes.

open_questions: How much of the gain comes from the LLM selection loop rather than from the memory structure? Baselines' read budgets are not stated, and CAM's context has no cap.

discussion.takeaway: Build reading memory as overlapping clusters stacked into summary levels, and let an LLM grow its evidence along that graph. In the paper this beats tree, graph and flat memories on six long-text tasks and lets new batches be added without a full rebuild.

claims.claim: Memory for reading agents should be structured, flexible (one unit feeds several abstractions) and dynamic (local updates).
CAM is best on all six datasets.
claims.evidence: Average +3.0% over the best baselines (RAPTOR, GraphRAG), e.g. NovelQA ACC-L 52.3 vs 47.8, ODSum-Meeting 50.7 vs 45.8. Table 2, §5.2

claims.claim: Letting a node join several clusters matters.
claims.evidence: RAPTOR (soft clusters) beats MemTree (strict tree) by 2.1% on average; removing node copies drops QMSum ACC-L 57.6 → 51.5. §5.2, Table 3

claims.claim: Prune-and-Grow beats both tree traversal and flat global retrieval over the same memory.
Batch insertion is fast and stable.
claims.evidence: Under 0.3h per 500-chunk batch vs 1.2h (RAPTOR) and 1.8h (GraphRAG) rebuilds; ACC-L stays roughly flat across batch sizes. Fig. 3, §5.3

claims.claim: Knowledge-graph extraction is not worth it on narratives but helps entity-rich QA.
claims.evidence: Table 3 row 8 (> 3× cost, small change); Table 7: 2Wiki EM 61.4 → 65.8 with it. §5.4, App. G

limits: Only tested on long-text reading comprehension.
Summary hallucinations can propagate to higher levels.
Assumes source texts are internally consistent.
The clustering algorithm is one of several possible implementations.
Prompts and hyperparameters are fixed by hand; nothing is learned from feedback.
reading: The released code has no incremental path: it rebuilds all levels from all chunks, so the online-batch timing and stability results (Fig. 3) cannot be checked against it.

Code defaults differ from the paper: 10 seed nodes instead of 5, text-embedding-3-large instead of -small, and α = θ = 0.6, outside the reported grids. The per-dataset settings used for Table 2 are not given.

The answer context is every node kept in any of up to 5 turns, with no size cap, and no token counts are reported; the paper does not state the baselines' retrieval budgets, so context size is not controlled.
The paper names GPT-4o as ACC-L judge; the code's judge function uses the same client as the reader (gpt-4o-mini by default).
Clusters larger than 12 are cut into consecutive slices of the member list, not by structure.
The summarisation script reads the 'gist' field by default, which summary nodes do not have (their text is stored as 'text'); the flags behind the QMSum and ODSum runs are not stated.
All baselines were rerun by the authors with GPT-4o-mini and text-embedding-3-small; FullContext has no multi-document numbers.
